structure.title: Frames and dissatisfaction
structure.text: The dedication and theatrical and heavenly prologues place Faust's private crisis within competing views of what the drama is doing.

structure.title: Experience and entanglement
structure.text: Faust's encounters move from dissatisfaction with learning into pleasures and relationships that involve lives beyond his own experiment.

people.name: Faust
people.text: An old scholar who has mastered every branch of learning and found it worthless, and who is ready to bargain with the devil for real experience.

people.name: Mephistopheles
people.text: The devil's agent, witty, cynical and endlessly obliging, who wagers that he can give Faust a moment he will want to last.

people.name: Gretchen
people.text: A young, devout girl Faust meets in the street, whose simple life is overturned by his pursuit of her.

context.title: A bargain with conditions
context.text: Different wagers and promises frame the action. Their exact terms matter more than the general phrase selling one's soul.

context.title: Part One
context.text: This is the first part of a larger work. Its mixture of lyric, comedy, argument, and drama is intentional.
context.takeaway: Let changes of form alter the pace.

notice.text: Notice who pays for Faust's renewed vitality.
notice.why: Another person's vulnerability can disappear inside his language of experience.
Wit can expose vanity while distracting from harm.

opening: Faust has studied everything he thought would make life worth living and finds himself trapped in a room full of books. He wants experience powerful enough to break through his disgust. Mephistopheles offers assistance, with terms attached, and the scholar's hunger acquires opportunities it has never had before. Goethe turns intellectual disappointment into a dangerous appetite for the world, where another person's innocence can become part of a man's experiment in finally feeling alive. The devil is excellent company while the costs accumulate.
